catalog_quote: Lobel & Riwarung 2011:38: "There are no phonemic geminates in Maranao, but consonants are phonetically longer following a schwa, e.g., tepad [təp.pad] 'get off a vehicle', tekaw [tək.kaw] 'startled, surprised', vs. likod [lɪ.kod] 'back (of body)', papag [pa.pag] 'wooden food cart' . Unlike Maguindanaon (Sullivan 1986:11), Maranao does not appear to have phonemic stress contrasts, but this deserves further inquiry as it is possible that the heavy consonants in Maranao affect stress patterns and that some underlying contrast may still be found." fn.9: "It is not at all uncommon for one or more members of a Philippine subgroup to have lost contrastive stress while others retain it ... It is also worth noting that most languages native to Mindanao and areas further south have lost contrastive stress." audit.reasoning: The record codes Maranao UNDETERMINED (no placement rule; stress apparently non-contrastive) on Lobel & Riwarung 2011 p.38 + fn.9 with McKaughan & Macaraya 1967 as a second leg. Both quotations were re-found verbatim at the stated places in the held files. The deciding source is the specialist modern phonological sketch, open and held as publisher PDF; the identical sentence recurs in Lobel's 2013 dissertation (p.287, fetched sources/held now), and Kaufman & Himmelmann's areal chapter cites that very passage as the state of knowledge, placing Mindanao languages loosely with the 'Eastern' (predictable penult) or 'Java' (no word stress) prototypes without resolving Maranao — which is exactly why UNDETERMINED rather than a penult or no-word-stress code is right. Allison 1979 (held) explicitly could not give stress data; Zorc 1993 does not list Maranao; Zorc's field-note bundle, McKaughan's 1958 int

sources.quote: 'Many if not most of the indigenous languages of Mindanao in the Philippines have no length distinction on roots and thus appear more compatible with the Eastern or Java prototype... As Lobel (2013:287) notes, Maranao does not appear to have stress contrasts but its sister language, Maguindanao does (Sullivan 1986:11).' (Eastern prototype = predictable penult, Java prototype = no word-level prominence; not resolved for Maranao.)

sources.citation: Lobel, Jason William. 2013. Philippine and North Bornean languages: issues in description, subgrouping, and reconstruction. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa.
sources.quote: 'Unlike Maguindanaon (Sullivan 1986:11), Maranao does not appear to have phonemic stress contrasts, but this deserves further inquiry as it is possible that the heavy consonants in Maranao affect stress patterns and that some underlying contrast may still be found.' fn.3: '...most languages native to Mindanao and areas further south have lost contrastive stress.' No placement rule anywhere in the chapter (only other stress hits in the diss are Manide/Alabat sec. 8.2.9 and the bibliography).

sources.quote: Introduction describes speakers, corpus (40,000 words of text from Dansalan/Marawi) and scope (verb inflection); 1996 grammatical sketch is morphosyntactic. Neither mentions stress or accent.
sources.locator: Introduction (1 p.); 1996 grammar sketch full djvu text
sources.note: Glottolog's only 'grammar' for Maranao; the 1967 dictionary intro we quote says 'a general statement of a more technical nature may be found elsewhere' pointing here, so if any early SIL statement of Maranao stress placement exists it is in this phonology section. Low odds of changing UNDETERMINED (same author defers in 1967), but it is the one primary not read in full.
